results.content: Therefore, implementing an AI pilot allows organizations to test AI solutions in a controlled setting, addressing these challenges before a full-scale rollout. ## What is an AI Pilot? Typically, an AI pilot addresses specific business challenges, such as automating repetitive tasks, enhancing decision-making, or improving customer experiences, while minimizing risks and investment costs. By starting with an AI Pilot, companies can test solutions on a smaller scale, identify potential challenges, and make necessary adjustments before a full-scale rollout. * **Example:** Roll out an AI chatbot for a subset of customers to gather initial performance data before scaling. * **Example:** After piloting an AI recommendation system, refine the algorithm based on customer feedback on the suggested products. * **Challenge:** Recent study identified scalability as the top challenge in transitioning AI projects from pilot to production This indicates that many pilots struggle to scale effectively due to technical limitations or inadequate infrastructure. * **Example:** A government agency might successfully test an AI model for data analytics on a small scale but find it difficult to manage increased data volumes or user demands when scaling up. * **Example:** An AI pilot designed to analyze customer feedback may falter if the input data includes unstructured text, images, and video without proper preprocessing. * **Example**: A tech startup may initiate an AI project but struggle to find data scientists or machine learning engineers to develop and refine their models. Develop a comprehensive data strategy that includes data cleansing, integration, and governance to ensure high-quality input for AI models. **Example**: A healthcare provider could pilot an AI tool in one department before rolling it out organization-wide based on initial success. ## Evaluating the AI Pilot’s Success To determine the success of an AI pilot, organizations need to assess it against clearly defined objectives and metrics. * Ensure the scaled solution adheres to relevant industry regulations, data privacy laws, and ethical AI guidelines. results.title: Defining Stopping Criteria in Large Language Models: A Practical Guide
results.content: # Defining Stopping Criteria in Large Language Models: A Practical Guide. Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4, Claude, and PaLM have transformed how we generate text, code, and even multi-turn conversations. But there’s one underrated piece of the generation puzzle that deeply affects how well these models perform: **stopping criteria**. Whether you're building a chatbot, a code assistant, or a text generation pipeline, you eventually need the model to stop generating tokens — at the right time. If it stops too early, your output might be incomplete. In this post, we’ll explore the different ways you can define stopping criteria for LLMs, with real-world examples and trade-offs. Limit the number of tokens the model can generate. ( model="gpt-4", messages=chat_history, max_tokens=512 ) ( model="gpt-4", messages=chat_history, max_tokens=512 ). Define one or more string sequences that, when generated, immediately stop further output. * Great for structured outputs like JSON, code blocks, or prompts with delimiters. ( model="gpt-4", messages=chat_history, stop=["\nHuman:", ""] ) ( model="gpt-4", messages=chat_history, stop=["\nHuman:", ""] ). Stop when the generated content semantically completes the task (e.g., completes a paragraph, finishes a function, etc.). if response.endswith((".", "!", "?")) and not continuation_needed(response): stop_generation = True if response.endswith((".", "!", "?")) and not continuation_needed(response): stop_generation = True. LLMs like GPT-4 and Claude can be guided with a schema — they stop generating when the function/tool-call is formed correctly. Use token sampling strategies to bias the model toward stopping earlier or reducing rambling. * Indirect — you’re guiding rather than explicitly stopping. ( model="gpt-4", messages=chat_history, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, presence_penalty=0.6 ) ( model="gpt-4", messages=chat_history, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, presence_penalty=0.6 ). If using token streaming, you can define your own logic to interrupt generation mid-way. def stop_streaming_callback(token): if token == "" or too_many_tokens_seen(): raise StopGeneration() # Used in streaming pipelines or async frameworks. def stop_streaming_callback(token): if token == "" or too_many_tokens_seen(): raise StopGeneration() # Used in streaming pipelines or async frameworks. ## 🧭 Wrapping Up. Stopping criteria isn’t just a technical detail — it shapes the user experience, performance, and reliability of your LLM-powered product. Whether you’re auto-generating code, writing product descriptions, or managing multi-turn dialogue, pick the criteria (or combo) that fits your use case.

results.title: Granular Codebook: Designs and Applications - Emergent Mind
results.content: * **Semantic and Cross-Modal Granular Codebooks**: For multi-modal learning, e.g., language-guided VQ (Liang et al., 23 May 2024) and text-augmented VQ (Liang et al., 3 Mar 2025), the granularity is defined by the ability to align codebook atoms not only with image features but with semantic or compositional linguistic representations at word, phrase, and sentence levels. Granular Codebooks in Communication Systems Granular codebooks have transformed classic communication system design, especially for high-dimensional MIMO, semantic communications, RIS configuration, and ultra-low bandwidth applications: * **Pilot-Efficient Feedback and Robustness**: By clustering channel realizations into granular regions using GMMs, feedback in FDD precoding is reduced to an index, obviating the need for pilot-intensive channel estimation at the mobile terminal (Turan et al., 2022). * **Digital Modulation Compatibility**: Multilevel granular codebooks such as MOC (multi-head octonary codebook) balance granularity with index compactness to align with digital signal constellations, enabling high-quality semantic communication at reduced channel bandwidth ratios (Zhou et al., 2 Jan 2024). * **Cross-Modal and Semantic-Granular Codebooks**: Recent work in LG-VQ (Liang et al., 23 May 2024) and TA-VQ (Liang et al., 3 Mar 2025) extends granularity into multi-modal and semantic dimensions, employing textual priors, multi-granularity alignment (at word/phrase/sentence levels), and sampling-based optimal transport losses to ground each code in fine-grained linguistic or compositional meaning. Granular codebooks are advantageous and often essential in applications requiring high discriminative resolution, adaptive control, or task-specific compactness: * **Massive MIMO and 5G/6G**: Enable pilot-efficient, feedback-minimal precoding and beam management even under highly scattering environments (Turan et al., 2022, Dreifuerst et al., 2023). results.title: Topical steroid withdrawal diagnostic criteria defined by NIH researchers | National Institutes of Health (NIH)
results.content: Hand and wrist of a participant in the pilot study before (left) and after (right) treatment of topical steroid withdrawal symptoms with berberine, a mitochondrial complex I-blocking drug.NIAID Researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) have determined that dermatitis resulting from topical steroid withdrawal (TSW) is distinct from eczema and is caused by an excess of an essential chemical compound in the body. The researchers then conducted a pilot study including 16 people with symptoms consistent with TSW, 10 people with eczema but no symptoms of TSW, and 11 people without skin disease. Additionally, the diagnostic criteria will help health care providers and researchers to better understand the prevalence of TSW and evaluate the effects of using topical steroids.
